3: And he to me: “This miserable mode Maintain the melancholy souls of those Who lived withouten infamy or praise.
7: Commingled are they with that caitiff choir Of Angels, who have not rebellious been, Nor faithful were to God, but were for self.
12: The heavens expelled them, not to be less fair; Nor them the nethermore abyss receives, For glory none the damned would have from them.”
17: And I: “O Master, what so grievous is To these, that maketh them lament so sore?” He answered: “I will tell thee very briefly.
22: These have no longer any hope of death; And this blind life of theirs is so debased, They envious are of every other fate.
26: No fame of them the world permits to be; Misericord and Justice both disdain them. Let us not speak of them, but look, and pass.”
31: And I, who looked again, beheld a banner, Which, whirling round, ran on so rapidly, That of all pause it seemed to me indignant;
36: And after it there came so long a train Of people, that I ne’er would have believed That ever Death so many had undone.
41: When some among them I had recognised, I looked, and I beheld the shade of him Who made through cowardice the great refusal.
47: Forthwith I comprehended, and was certain, That this the sect was of the caitiff wretches Hateful to God and to his enemies.
52: These miscreants, who never were alive, Were naked, and were stung exceedingly By gadflies and by hornets that were there.
56: These did their faces irrigate with blood, Which, with their tears commingled, at their feet By the disgusting worms was gathered up.
61: And when to gazing farther I betook me. People I saw on a great river’s bank; Whence said I: “Master, now vouchsafe to me,
66: That I may know who these are, and what law Makes them appear so ready to pass over, As I discern athwart the dusky light.”
71: And he to me: “These things shall all be known To thee, as soon as we our footsteps stay Upon the dismal shore of Acheron.”
76: Then with mine eyes ashamed and downward cast, Fearing my words might irksome be to him, From speech refrained I till we reached the river.
81: And lo! towards us coming in a boat An old man, hoary with the hair of eld, Crying: “Woe unto you, ye souls depraved!
85: Hope nevermore to look upon the heavens; I come to lead you to the other shore, To the eternal shades in heat and frost.
90: And thou, that yonder standest, living soul, Withdraw thee from these people, who are dead!” But when he saw that I did not withdraw,
95: He said: “By other ways, by other ports Thou to the shore shalt come, not here, for passage; A lighter vessel needs must carry thee.”
100: And unto him the Guide: “Vex thee not, Charon; It is so willed there where is power to do That which is willed; and farther question not.”
105: Thereat were quieted the fleecy cheeks Of him the ferryman of the livid fen, Who round about his eyes had wheels of flame.
110: But all those souls who weary were and naked Their colour changed and gnashed their teeth together, As soon as they had heard those cruel words.
115: God they blasphemed and their progenitors, The human race, the place, the time, the seed Of their engendering and of their birth!
120: Thereafter all together they drew back, Bitterly weeping, to the accursed shore, Which waiteth every man who fears not God.
125: Charon the demon, with the eyes of glede, Beckoning to them, collects them all together, Beats with his oar whoever lags behind.
130: As in the autumn-time the leaves fall off, First one and then another, till the branch Unto the earth surrenders all its spoils;
135: In similar wise the evil seed of Adam Throw themselves from that margin one by one, At signals, as a bird unto its lure.
141: So they depart across the dusky wave, And ere upon the other side they land, Again on this side a new troop assembles.
144: “My son,” the courteous Master said to me, “All those who perish in the wrath of God Here meet together out of every land;
149: And ready are they to pass o’er the river, Because celestial Justice spurs them on, So that their fear is turned into desire.
150: This way there never passes a good soul; And hence if Charon doth complain of thee, Well mayst thou know now what his speech imports.”
152: This being finished, all the dusk champaign Trembled so violently, that of that terror The recollection bathes me still with sweat.
153: The land of tears gave forth a blast of wind, And fulminated a vermilion light, Which overmastered in me every sense,
154:
And as a man whom sleep hath seized I fell.

Inferno: Canto IV
155: Broke the deep lethargy within my head A heavy thunder, so that I upstarted, Like to a person who by force is wakened;
156: And round about I moved my rested eyes, Uprisen erect, and steadfastly I gazed, To recognise the place wherein I was.
157: True is it, that upon the verge I found me Of the abysmal valley dolorous, That gathers thunder of infinite ululations.
158: Obscure, profound it was, and nebulous, So that by fixing on its depths my sight Nothing whatever I discerned therein.
160: “Let us descend now into the blind world,” Began the Poet, pallid utterly; “I will be first, and thou shalt second be.”
163: And I, who of his colour was aware, Said: “How shall I come, if thou art afraid, Who’rt wont to be a comfort to my fears?”
